Coupling
KUP-ling
noun
From the Latin copula, a bond or tie, through the Old French copler — the joining of two things into one. In Exodus it is the technical term for the seam where two sets of tabernacle curtains are joined.

Biblical Definition

The coupling is a seam, and the Holy Ghost spends an extraordinary number of verses on it. “Thou shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of the one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling” (Exo 26:4); fifty loops answering fifty loops, “that the loops may take hold one of another”; then “fifty taches of gold, and couple the curtains together with the taches: and it shall be one tabernacle” (Exo 26:6). Over the tent of goats’ hair, the same again in brass: “put the taches into the loops, and couple the tent together, that it may be one” (Exo 26:11). The refrain is unmistakable — that it may be one. Ten curtains, and the chapter will not rest until they are a single dwelling. Nothing in the tabernacle was designed by a committee of preference; every loop was counted and every clasp specified, because the house where God met His people had to be one house. The New Testament takes the figure up without apology: the church is a building fitly framed together, growing unto an holy temple in the Lord, “from whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth” (Eph 4:16). The couplings are the joints, and the strength of the whole is measured at the seams — which is exactly where a fabric tears.

Webster 1828 Definition

The seam or joining where two curtains are united; that which couples or fastens things together into one.

COUPLING, n. That which couples or connects; the joining of two things.

The place or seam where two breadths are united.

From the Latin copula, a band or tie; Old French copler, to join.

In the tabernacle, the seam at which the sets of curtains were joined by loops and taches (Exo 26:4–6).

In mechanics, the contrivance connecting one part or carriage with another.

Key Scripture

Exo 26:4 — "And thou shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of the one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling; and likewise shalt thou make in the uttermost edge of another curtain, in the coupling of the second."

Exo 26:6 — "And thou shalt make fifty taches of gold, and couple the curtains together with the taches: and it shall be one tabernacle."

Exo 26:11 — "And thou shalt make fifty taches of brass, and put the taches into the loops, and couple the tent together, that it may be one."

Eph 4:16 — "From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part , maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love."

Modern Corruption

Church unity is pursued either by doctrinal indifference or abandoned altogether for private religion — where the tabernacle shows a unity that is designed, specified, fastened, and costly.

expand to see more

The corruption runs to two extremes, and the couplings rebuke both. On one side is the unity that is purchased by subtraction, in which the loops are loosened and the taches thrown away so that anyone may be joined to anything, and the resulting fabric is one only in the sense that a heap is one. Scripture’s unity is nothing like that: fifty loops must answer fifty loops exactly, blue to blue, edge to edge, or the curtains do not meet. On the other side is the private Christianity that treats the seam as optional, holding that a man may be joined to Christ while joined to no congregation — a curtain persuaded it is a tabernacle. Exodus counts the loops precisely because a dwelling is not a collection of hangings.

Recover the plain sense: unity is a designed thing, specified by God, and it is fastened at cost — taches of gold for the inner curtains, taches of brass for the outer. The refrain that it may be one is the point of the whole chapter, and it culminates in our Lord’s prayer that they all may be one. Then take Eph 4:16 as the working principle: the body is compacted by that which every joint supplieth, which means the seams are where the labour is. Congregational life is largely the maintenance of couplings — bearing with one another, forgiving, keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace — and a fabric always tears at the seam, which is precisely why the loops were counted.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin copula, a bond — the seam joining curtain to curtain, until the refrain is answered: that it may be one.

expand to see more

Coupling — Latin copula, a tie; Old French copler, to join.

In Exodus, the seam where two sets of curtains are united.

Fifty loops answering fifty loops, fastened by taches of gold and of brass.

The refrain of Exo 26 is that it may be one (vv. 6, 11).

Eph 4:16: the body compacted by that which every joint supplieth.

Usage

"The loops must answer exactly — unity by specification, not by subtraction."

"Gold taches within, brass without: the joining is costly at every layer."

"A fabric tears at the seam, which is why the couplings are counted."
